list.listitem: Order imaging in adults with acute trauma, those with suspicion of malignancy (eg, age, history of cancer, weight loss), and patients with persistent symptoms after conservative treatment. C
MRI is the preferred study if clinical suspicion of osseous or surrounding tissue abnormality is high and plain radiographs are inconclusive. C
Order X-rays in children and adolescents complaining of pain in hip, thigh, or knee, or of limping to evaluate the possibility of Legg-Perthes syndrome or slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). C
Aspirate the joint in suspected arthritis or suspected protesthetic hip joint infection. C

background.definition: Hip pain can be a diagnostic challenge as the pain may originate from hip joint, surrounding tissues/bones, as well as referred pain. Hip pain may be musculoskeletal in nature or caused by infection, neoplasia, or other processes.

list.listitem: Each year, hip pain accounts for about 1% of all visits to family physicians.
In the general population, the prevalence of hip pain is 10% and increases with age. Of patients who are 60 years or older, about 14% report hip pain on most days.
Among patients with hip pain seen in primary care, more than one-third have radiographic evidence of degenerative joint disease.
In the United States, about 25% of adults over 45 years of age have X-ray evidence of osteoarthritis of the hips. About 10% are symptomatic.
The rate of radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis approaches 80% in persons more than 75 years of age.
About 1% of the adult population has rheumatoid arthritis.
Among 3541 infants undergoing screening ultrasonography of their hips, the overall frequency of hip dysplasia was about 5%.

Musculoskeletal: fracture, avascular necrosis of the femoral head, gluteal tendinopathy, strains/tendonitis, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis. Approximately 14% of patients with hip pain have tears or tendinosis of the gluteal medius or minimus. Among patients with hip pain, after evaluation, about 15% have greater trochanteric pain syndrome.
Infectious: septicarthritis, osteomyelitis, regional cellulitis.
Congential: Legg-Calve-Perthes syndrome, SCFE, developmental dysplasia of the hip, various neurologic disorders.
Other: piriformis syndrome, bursitis, labral tears, metastatic cancer.
Nonhip-joint-related pain (ie, referred pain): appendicitis, inguinal hernias, renal colic, sacroiliitis, inflammatory bowel disease, colon tumors, gynecologic disorders.
Among 144 consecutive children evaluated for hip pain, 40% had transient synovitis, 15% had Legg-Perthes syndrome, and 3% had SCFE.
Avascular necrosis: interruption of blood flow to bone matrix leading to bone infarction.
Osteoarthritis: decrease in hyaluronic acid due to reduced production leading to mechanical deformation, joint contracture, and joint instability.
Rheumatoid arthritis: likely due to inflammation of synovial membrane and articular structure.
Septic arthritis: infective arthritis due to direct microorganism invasion of joint space.

Differential.Differential_Features: Limited range of motion, morning stiffness, pain with weight bearing
History of trauma followed by inability to walk, limb externally rotated, intense pain
Dull ache in groin, thigh, or buttock; limited range of motion, history of corticosteroid or alcohol use
Fever, chills, inability to bear weight
Pain over lateral hip or greater trochanter, sudden onset

list.listitem: Osteoarthritis: Among patients with severe degenerative joint disease of the hip, over 80% have pain in the groin and nearly half have symptoms below the knee.A systematic review of 6 high quality studies that included a total of 1110 patients found that family history of OA (LR+ 2.1), personal history of knee OA (LR+ 2.1), pain climbing stairs or walking up slopes (LR+ 2.1) and the worst pain in the medial thigh (LR+ 7.8) were associated with the presence of hip OA. Findings associated with not having OA included being younger than 60 years, morning stiffness <60 minutes, no pain with walking, and pain not improved by sitting. Physical findings associated with hip OA included posterior hip pain with squatting, groin pain on hip ab- or adduction, abductor weakness, and decreased internal rotation.

Labral tear: Hyperabduction, twisting, falling are common mechanisms of injury for a labral tear. Among patients with labral tears of the acetabulum, about half present with insidious symptoms; over 90% complain primarily of anterior hip or groin pain and pain worse with activity. About 70% have pain at night. Among patients with a labral tear of the acetabulum confirmed by arthroscopy, 38% also had an abnormal Trendelenberg test (see below). In patients with an abnormal FABER test (below), the most common problem identified on arthroscopy was labral tear.

FABER test: To perform the FABER (flexion, abduction, and external rotation) or Patrick test, while the patient is supine, flex the affected leg, and then abduct and externally rotate it. Apply gentle downward pressure along the medial aspect of the knee toward the table. Among patients undergoing hip arthroscopy, 88% of those with abnormal FABER tests had abnormal findings on arthroscopy, most commonly a torn labrum. Pain in the sacroiliac region with this maneuver suggests sacroiliac joint problems.

Iliotibial band syndrome: To perform the Ober test, the patient lies on the unaffected side with the unaffected hip and knee flexed to 90°. The upper hip (affected) is passively extended while keeping the knee at 90° and lowered to the table. Inability to adduct the leg or lateral knee pain may indicate iliotibial band syndrome.

Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis): Suspect this condition in patients with hip pain who are taking corticosteroids, have a hemoglobinopathy, history of hip dislocation or femoral neck fracture, or collagen vascular disease. Patients may present with acute, subacute, or chronic onset of pain, and pain may range from mild to severe.

Gluteus medius tear or weakness: In the Trendelenberg test, the patient stands on the affected leg. The test is abnormal if the pelvis on the opposite side drops. In evaluating patients with hip pain who underwent MRI, the Trendelenberg test was more sensitive (73%) and specific (77%) in the diagnosis of gluteus medius tear than the FABER test (73% and 46%, respectively). The risk factors for gluteal tears include age related deteriorations, female sex and increased BMI. A study identified 8 million patient charts of patients who had evidence of a lumbar spine diagnosis, had received lumbar injections or surgery. They found that 5.4% had gluteal tears, representing a relative risk of 13.6, suggesting a strong association between lumbar spine pathology and abductor tears.

Gluteal tendinopathy: A small study (n = 65) evaluated clinical maneuvers to diagnose gluteal tendinopathy in patients with lateral hip pain, using MRI as the reference standard. If a patient reported pain within 30 seconds of standing on the affected limb, that increased the likelihood of gluteal tendinopathy from 50% to 98%. On the other hand, the absence of pain on palpation of the greater trochanter significantly reduced the likelihood of gluteal tendinopathy.
Obturator hernia: a relatively rare cause of hip pain, it is typically seen in debilitated older women and is accompanied by pain radiating down the medial high and knee (Howship-Romberg sign).

Femoroacetabular impingement syndrome: The impingement test involves having the patient bring their knee up towards their chest and then rotating it inward towards their opposite shoulder. If this causes the pain it suggests impingement.

Septic arthritis (adults): joint pain (85%), a history of joint swelling (78%), and fever (57%) are the only clinical clues that occur in more than 50% of adult patients with septic arthritis.The presence of skin infection, especially in a patient with hip or knee prosthesis, is strong evidence in favor of septic arthritis, as is recent joint surgery or age older than 80 years.

Congenital hip dysplasia: To conduct Ortolani's maneuver for hip dysplasia, place the infant on its back and flex the hips. With your thumbs placed on the medial aspect of each knee and remaining finger tips over the hips, gently abduct the hips. Grade 1 instability involves slight capsular instability but no snapping or limitation of movement. Grade 2 is when the hip is subluxable with snapping. Grade 3 is when the hip is dislocatable and reducible. Grade 4 is fully dislocated and not reducible. Compared with ultrasound, the Ortolani maneuver for hip dysplasia in infants is about 97% sensitive but only about 14% specific.

Hip pain in children: Young children with hip problems may limp and complain of pain in their knee. Most of these children will have a transient synovitis. To distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip in children, see clinical decision rule below. Among children with SCFE, about 15% complain of distal thigh or knee pain.

An association has been established between chronic pain and the degree of frailty. A bidirectional Mendelian randomization study concluded that a higher frailty index and yjr Fried Frailty Score were associated with chronic pain. Interestingly, the authors found that chronic pain was also associated with frailty, making this a bidirectional relationship which can coexist and exacerbate one another.

Plain radiographs are the initial imaging study for most adults and children patients with hip pain. In adults with chronic hip pain in whom X-rays are negative, MRI is the recommended study if labral tear, osteonecrosis, or other osseous or soft tissue abnormalities are suspected. Injection with anesthetic is recommended to confirm mild osteoarthritis as the cause of pain, and CT is the recommended imaging study in patients with suspected osteoid osteoma. In children with suspected septic arthritis, ultrasound may be helpful in localizing an effusion.

If hip fracture is clinically suspected despite normal radiographs, elderly patients should undergo CT, bone scan or MRI. A protocol of CT first followed by MRI only if necessary successfully reduced cost and improved efficiency of care. A second study supported a good negative predictive value of negative CT for suspected occult hip fracture (96%). A systematic review identified 35 studies with 2992 patients that evaluated the role of CT or MRI in elderly patients with hip pains and clinical signs and symptoms that suggest fracture but normal radiographs. Overall, 39% has an occult surgical hip fracture detected in studies with no definite radiographic fracture, and 92% in studies of patients with radiographic evidence suggesting an isolated greater trochanteric fracture. Occult fracture was higher in those with a history of trauma and those over 80 years. In comparison with MRI as the reference standard, the sensitivity of CT was 79% and of bone scan was 87%.

Two large cohort studies compared radiographic findings with symptoms. The Framingham Osteoarthritis Study (n = 946) found that only 16% of hips in patients with frequent hip pain had radiographic evidence of OA, while only 21% of those with radiographic hip OA had frequent hip pain.The osteoarthritis Initiative study had similar findings.
Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis): if clinically suspected, plain radiographs are the initial study, followed by MRI if xray is inconclusive or if surgery is being contemplated.

Trauma: In 100 (mostly elderly) patients with persistent hip pain after trauma whose initial radiographs were normal, subsequent MRI found 46 occult femoral neck or intertrochanteric fractures and 27 other fractures.

Labral and other cartilage tears: Compared with arthroscopy, the sensitivity of MR arthrography is between 71% and 100%, and the specificity is between 44% and 80% in diagnosing labral tears; it is 47% sensitive and 89% specific in diagnosing articular cartilage pathology.
Loose body: Compared with arthroscopy, MR arthrography is quite specific in detecting articular loose bodies (96%), but is only 44% sensitive.

Septic arthritis: If suspected clinically (ie, fever, chills, recent surgery, skin infection, joint replacement), obtain CBC, sedimentation rate or CRP, and synovial fluid for cell counts, glucose, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels. Progressively higher synovial WBC counts strongly increase the likelihood of septic arthritis, as do low glucose and elevated LDH.

Hip pain (young child): Young children with hip problems may limp and complain of pain in their knee. Most of these children will have a transient synovitis, but order X-rays of their hip, femur, and knee. See validated clinical rule, which uses CBC, sedimentation rate, and symptoms to distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis.

Hip pain (older child): Older children and adolescents complaining of pain in the hip, thigh, or knee or of limping should have X-rays to evaluate the possibility of Legg-Perthes syndrome or SCFE. Ultrasound of the hip is about 71% sensitive and 99% specific in the diagnosis of suspected Legg-Perthes syndrome.

Femoroacetabular impingement syndrome: This is a structural cause of hip pain in young adults caused by bone spurs that limit range of motion and cause pain. It is generally diagnosed based on the history, physical and radiography; advanced imaging is not generally needed. An injection of anesthetic agent causing relief of pain also suggests the diagnosis.

Congenital hip dysplasia: For evaluation of an infant for congenital hip dysplasia, initial imaging is ultrasound. In a small randomized trial of infants with clinical hip instability, those evaluated with ultrasound were less likely to be splinted (37%) or have surgery (7%) compared with infants managed by clinical evaluation alone (48% and 8%, respectively).

The presence of peripheral arterial disease (PAD) may be a cofactor in the loss of function among patients with OA. In a study of 22 patients, PAD (range of ABI 0.28-0.82) in patients with symptoms ranging from mild claudication to rest pain was associated with lower hip extensor strength, shorter walking distances in the 6 minute walk test, and poorer balance on a single leg.

A clinical decision rule has been developed and validated to determine the likelihood of septic arthritis in children with hip pain. It requires a sedimentation rate and CBC, as well as recent symptoms.
See for a suggested approach to evaluating the adult with hip pain.

History of cancer, weight loss, or night pain?
Steroid use, heavy alcohol use, sickle cell disease, or past fracture or dislocation?
Where is the pain?
cell.path: Groin pain, stiffness, and painful internal rotation, age 45 or older
Lateral hip pain with tenderness over the greater trochanter
Groin pain with clicking or catching in a younger, active adult

cell.label: X-ray (AP pelvis and lateral hip). If negative but unable to bear weight, MRI for occult fracture.
Suspect septic arthritis or prosthetic joint infection. ESR, CRP, joint aspiration; urgent orthopedic referral.
X-ray; MRI if negative to evaluate for metastasis or primary bone tumor.
X-ray; noncontrast MRI if negative to rule out avascular necrosis.
Hip osteoarthritis. Clinical diagnosis; X-ray only if uncertain. Exercise, weight loss, NSAIDs.
Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (gluteal tendinopathy). Exercise therapy; injection if needed.
Femoroacetabular impingement or labral tear. X-ray, physical therapy; MRI arthrogram if it persists.
Consider stress fracture (runners, osteoporosis), hernia, or abdominal or pelvic causes. MRI if pain persists.

footnotes.footnote: Hip pain may be referred from the lumbar spine, abdomen, or pelvis.
Hip arthroscopy has limited benefit for degenerative disease.
